verses.text: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel.
The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Eleazar became the father of Phinehas, Phinehas became the father of Abishua,
Abishua became the father of Bukki. Bukki became the father of Uzzi.
Uzzi became the father of Zerahiah. Zerahiah became the father of Meraioth.
Meraioth became the father of Amariah. Amariah became the father of Ahitub.
Ahitub became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Ahimaaz.
Ahimaaz became the father of Azariah. Azariah became the father of Johanan.
Johanan became the father of Azariah, who executed the priest’s office in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem.
Azariah became the father of Amariah. Amariah became the father of Ahitub.
Ahitub became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Shallum.
Shallum became the father of Hilkiah. Hilkiah became the father of Azariah.
Azariah became the father of Seraiah. Seraiah became the father of Jehozadak.
Jehozadak went into captivity, when Yahweh carried Judah and Jerusalem away by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari.
These are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the families of the Levites according to their fathers’ households.
Of Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son,
Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, and Jeatherai his son.
The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son,
Elkanah his son, and Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son,
Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son.
The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth.
As for Elkanah, the sons of Elkanah: Zophai his son, Nahath his son,
Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, and Elkanah his son.
The sons of Samuel: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah.
The sons of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son,
Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son.
These are they whom David set over the service of song in Yahweh’s house, after the ark came to rest there.
They ministered with song before the tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting, until Solomon had built Yahweh’s house in Jerusalem. They performed the duties of their office according to their order.
These are those who served, and their sons. Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman the singer, the son of Joel, the son of Samuel,
the son of Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Eliel, the son of Toah,
the son of Zuph, the son of Elkanah, the son of Mahath, the son of Amasai,
the son of Elkanah, the son of Joel, the son of Azariah, the son of Zephaniah,
the son of Tahath, the son of Assir, the son of Ebiasaph, the son of Korah,
the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, the son of Israel.
His brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berechiah, the son of Shimea,
the son of Michael, the son of Baaseiah, the son of Malchijah,
the son of Ethni, the son of Zerah, the son of Adaiah,
the son of Ethan, the son of Zimmah, the son of Shimei,
the son of Jahath, the son of Gershom, the son of Levi.
On the left hand their brothers the sons of Merari: Ethan the son of Kishi, the son of Abdi, the son of Malluch,
the son of Hashabiah, the son of Amaziah, the son of Hilkiah,
the son of Amzi, the son of Bani, the son of Shemer,
the son of Mahli, the son of Mushi, the son of Merari, the son of Levi.
Their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of God’s house.

But Aaron and his sons offered on the altar of burnt offering, and on the altar of incense, for all the work of the most holy place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.
These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son,
Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son,
Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son,
Zadok his son, and Ahimaaz his son.
Now these are their dwelling places according to their encampments in their borders: to the sons of Aaron, of the families of the Kohathites (for theirs was the first lot),
to them they gave Hebron in the land of Judah, and its suburbs around it;
but the fields of the city, and its villages, they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
To the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge, Hebron; Libnah also with its suburbs, Jattir, Eshtemoa with its suburbs,
Hilen with its suburbs, Debir with its suburbs,
Ashan with its suburbs, and Beth Shemesh with its suburbs;
and out of the tribe of Benjamin, Geba with its suburbs, Allemeth with its suburbs, and Anathoth with its suburbs. All their cities throughout their families were thirteen cities.
To the rest of the sons of Kohath were given by lot, out of the family of the tribe, out of the half-tribe, the half of Manasseh, ten cities.

To the sons of Gershom, according to their families, out of the tribe of Issachar, and out of the tribe of Asher, and out of the tribe of Naphtali, and out of the tribe of Manasseh in Bashan, thirteen cities.
To the sons of Merari were given by lot, according to their families, out of the tribe of Reuben, and out of the tribe of Gad, and out of the tribe of Zebulun, twelve cities.
The children of Israel gave to the Levites the cities with their suburbs.
They gave by lot out of the tribe of the children of Judah, and out of the tribe of the children of Simeon, and out of the tribe of the children of Benjamin, these cities which are mentioned by name.
Some of the families of the sons of Kohath had cities of their borders out of the tribe of Ephraim.
They gave to them the cities of refuge, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim with its suburbs; Gezer also with its suburbs,
Jokmeam with its suburbs, Beth Horon with its suburbs,
Aijalon with its suburbs, Gath Rimmon with its suburbs;
and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner with its suburbs, and Bileam with its suburbs, for the rest of the family of the sons of Kohath.
To the sons of Gershom were given, out of the family of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Golan in Bashan with its suburbs, and Ashtaroth with its suburbs;
and out of the tribe of Issachar, Kedesh with its suburbs, Daberath with its suburbs,
Ramoth with its suburbs, and Anem with its suburbs;
and out of the tribe of Asher, Mashal with its suburbs, Abdon with its suburbs,
Hukok with its suburbs, and Rehob with its suburbs;
and out of the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee with its suburbs, Hammon with its suburbs, and Kiriathaim with its suburbs.
To the rest of the Levites, the sons of Merari, were given, out of the tribe of Zebulun, Rimmono with its suburbs, Tabor with its suburbs;
and beyond the Jordan at Jericho, on the east side of the Jordan, were given them, out of the tribe of Reuben, Bezer in the wilderness with its suburbs, and Jahzah with its suburbs,
Kedemoth with its suburbs, and Mephaath with its suburbs;
and out of the tribe of Gad, Ramoth in Gilead with its suburbs, Mahanaim with its suburbs,
Heshbon with its suburbs, and Jazer with its suburbs.

footnotes.content: Three sons—Gershon, Kohath, Merari—set the pattern for Levi's whole family line. From these three branches came all those who would keep the Tabernacle's service. What a gift, to come from a calling that runs this deep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Kohathites were the priestly branch, and look who stands here as the main trunk: Amram himself. His children would shake the world—Aaron the first high priest, Moses the lawgiver, Miriam the prophet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam—siblings who each carried their own calling, yet bound by the same redemptive story. Aaron's four sons begin the priestly succession, though two would stumble in the wilderness. The Lord makes all these names permanent here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watch the priesthood pass down through Eleazar's line, solid and steady. Phinehas steps into his father's office and becomes known for zeal—he runs toward the altar when others might flee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bukki and Uzzi—names that echo with faithful service, though we hear them only here. Yet the Lord kept them in His eye, generation to generation, priest after priest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priestly line marches on: Zerahiah to Meraioth, one hand passing to the next. This is what continuity looks like—not glamorous, but necessary, each man learning his father's trade of standing between God and His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amariah, Ahitub—they come and go in the record, yet they held the line. When a man accepts the priesthood, he becomes a link in a chain meant to last forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok appears here as the heir of a long priestly succession. He would become David's faithful high priest, a man so trustworthy that kings consulted him. The genealogy shows us his true pedigree: straight through Eleazar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahimaaz becomes Zadok's heir, continuing a priesthood rooted in faithfulness. These aren't just names—they're links to men who bore the Urim and Thummim, who stood in the Holy Place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Azariah performs the priesthood in Solomon's Temple—a pivotal note marking the shift from wilderness to a permanent house of prayer. After centuries of wandering, the worship finally settles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The line continues unbroken into Solomon's era and beyond. Amariah and Ahitub—their names repeat (we've heard them before), yet they're new men in a new age. God's purposes span generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok appears again—this branch of his line survives and prospers. A priest who kept his integrity through court intrigue and dynastic strife was rare and precious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hilkiah and Azariah—faithful men whose names echo through the kingdom's history. In the reforms to come, one of Hilkiah's descendants will discover the Book of the Law itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seraiah and Jehozadak—the line stretches forward toward exile. Yet even here, the priesthood isn't broken; it continues in captivity and waits for restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehozadak was carried away when Nebuchadnezzar conquered Jerusalem—yet this verse preserves his name and his priesthood survives the rupture. The exile is not the end; it is a pause in a story that resumes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The record restarts the three sons of Levi—Gershom, Kohath, Merari. This time we'll hear from the singers and musicians, those who served not with the knife and censer but with voice and instrument.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gershom's branch splits into Libni and Shimei. From these two lines came David's musicians—men like Asaph, whose songs still echo in our worship today.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Kohathites are named again, now as the family from which singers arose. When David brought the ark to Jerusalem, it was Kohathites who sang and played.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The three families of Levi are bound by blood and calling—Mahli and Mushi of Merari, the youngest branch. Yet the Lord honored each family's gift for service.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Libni begins the descent through Gershom's line—Jahath, Zimmah, each man a link in the chain of worship. These aren't just ancestors; they're the roots of David's own singers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The genealogy runs through Joah, Iddo, Zerah, Jeatherai—each one part of the Gershonite stream. How many of these men spent their whole lives learning and teaching the songs?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the Kohathites: Amminadab to Korah to Assir—lines within lines. Korah himself had a famous end (he rebelled in the wilderness), yet his descendants were honored to serve in song.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elkanah appears here—the great-grandfather of Samuel, though we don't meet Samuel until later. Yet here he is, part of the music and worship of the Tabernacle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, Shaul—the Kohathite line continues. These men inherited the gift of song and the duty to shepherd Israel's worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elkanah's sons—Amasai and Ahimoth—both musicians and servants. From Elkanah's line would come Samuel himself, the prophet-judge who would anoint Israel's kings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zophai and Nahath—Elkanah's descendants in the line of singers. Each name represents a man who carried the calling forward, though he may be remembered only in genealogy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliab, Jeroham, Elkanah—the names compress generations into a handful of verses. Yet each one lived, loved, served, and passed the torch forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samuel the prophet comes from this line of singers—Joel his father, Elkanah before that, all the way back to Kohath himself. A boy born in a barren woman's hope, a man who would reshape Israel's kingship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Merari's branch—Mahli, Libni, Shimei, Uzzah—the third family of singers. These men stood ready to lift the music higher when David's heart was moved to praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimea, Haggiah, Asaiah—the Merarite line stretches forward, each man part of the music corps that would serve in Solomon's Temple and beyond.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the ark came to rest—a turning point. David chose these singers and musicians to lead worship in the Tabernacle, not out of mere ceremony but from joy and reverence toward the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sang and served through the Tent of Meeting's centuries, then transitioned into Solomon's Temple. Not a break in worship, but a deepening—a people learning to sing their faith to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Heman the singer emerges—a giant of Israel's music, descended from Samuel, crowned with wisdom by the Lord. Here is the culmination of the Kohathite singers, tracing back through generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The genealogy winds back: from Heman to Elkanah to Jeroham to Eliel—each link in the great chain that produces the chief musician of David's court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zuph, Elkanah, Mahath, Amasai—names in the shadow, yet they stood in the light once. Their faithfulness in obscurity bore fruit in Heman's great ministry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The line spirals deeper into time: Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, Zephaniah—all funneling down to one man, Heman, who would become the voice of Israel's praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, Korah—the lineage passes through Korah, the rebel who perished in the wilderness, yet his descendants rose to sing in the very house Korah refused to serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Izhar, Kohath, Levi, Israel—the genealogy traces all the way back to the patriarchs, rooting Heman's gift in the family of the covenant itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asaph stands on Heman's right hand—second among the singers, brother-in-service. His psalms fill the Psalter even today; his voice echoes across centuries of worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Michael, Baaseiah, Malchijah—Asaph's ancestors stretch backward, each one a note in the chord that produces this great musician.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ethni, Zerah, Adaiah—the line continues back, branch after branch, all converging in Asaph's gift for music and prophecy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ethan, Zimmah, Shimei—the genealogy spirals deeper, showing how Asaph too descended from the singers of old, heir to a tradition as ancient as Levi himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jahath, Gershom, Levi—Asaph's line traces back to the very roots. By blood and calling, he is Gershom's heir, a keeper of the family's sacred music.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ethan of the Merarites stands on the left hand—a second great musician, descended from Merari's branch. Where Heman led from strength and Asaph from prophecy, Ethan offered the praise of the third family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hashabiah, Amaziah, Hilkiah—Ethan's ancestors reach back into Merari's line, each one part of the weaving that brings this master musician into being.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amzi, Bani, Shemer—the Merarite stream flows on, carrying music and worship forward, generation to generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mahli, Mushi, Merari, Levi—Ethan's line too traces back to the patriarchs, confirming that all three branches of Levite singers are rooted in the same deep covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The other Levites served everywhere—carrying the Tabernacle, maintaining its rituals, keeping the house of God. Not all were singers; all were essential.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron and his sons alone offered at the altars—the sacred boundary between priest and people, forever. The most holy work was theirs, atonement for Israel their calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eleazar begins the restatement of Aaron's priestly line, a return to the theme of the chapter's opening. The priesthood and the music—twin streams of Levite service.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah—the priestly succession flows on. Each priest was a custodian of atonement and intercession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Meraioth, Amariah, Ahitub—more links in the high-priestly chain that stretched from Aaron through centuries of Israelite faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zadok, Ahimaaz—Zadok we know as David's priest, a man of faithfulness and wisdom who never wavered. His son Ahimaaz served under him, carrying forward the priestly office.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the record turns to homes—the places where priests and Levites would dwell. The Lord didn't just give them calling; He gave them land, security, provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron—the city of refuge and the center of Aaron's inheritance. How fitting: the city where David ruled, where wisdom gathered, became the priestly city.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the fields around Hebron went to Caleb, the faithful spy. A reminder that the priests weren't to own all the land—the Lord reserved portions for those who proved faithful in their own trials.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cities of refuge—Hebron, Libnah, Jattir, Eshtemoa—places of mercy where the manslayer could flee. The priests lived where safety itself was sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hilen, Debir—each city a home for priestly families, each one an outpost of the Lord's mercy and order throughout Judah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ashan, Beth Shemesh—more cities where priests could settle and raise their children in the faith. The Lord didn't scatter them randomly but gave them real homes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirteen cities for the Kohathites—a full inheritance scattered across Judah and Benjamin. The number thirteen reminds us the pattern extends throughout all Israel's tribes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten cities given to the rest of the Kohathites from Manasseh—the Lord's provision extended beyond Judah's borders into the heartland.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gershomites received thirteen cities scattered across Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Bashan—the northern tribes blessed with priests in their midst to lead worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Merarites received twelve cities—Reuben, Gad, Zebulun—again a pattern that shows the Lord distributed His servants throughout all Israel's landscape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people of Israel gave these cities to the Levites—not by compulsion but as part of the covenant's design, a voluntary sharing of inheritance with those who served the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah, Simeon, Benjamin—each tribe contributed cities where Levites would dwell and minister. Unity in worship required the whole people to support the servants of the altar.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the families of Kohath received portions in Ephraim—the central tribe, where wisdom and leadership often gathered. The priests weren't confined to Judah alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shechem—a city heavy with history, where Jacob's sons once committed violence, where Joshua's covenant was renewed. Now it becomes a refuge city and a priestly dwelling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jokmeam, Beth Horon—cities known as military strongholds, now also centers of worship and priestly ministry. The Lord sanctified all of Israel's landscape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aijalon, Gath Rimmon—places that would see conflict and history, yet they remained priestly cities, refuges of grace amid the world's tumult.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aner, Bileam in Manasseh—the Lord's provision extended to the half-tribe, ensuring the priestly family had secure places to worship and serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Gershomites received Golan in Bashan—a city of refuge where the avenger's justice couldn't reach the innocent, guarded by priests who understood mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kedesh, Daberath in Issachar—each city a lighthouse of faith in the northern territories, where singers and servers kept the Lord's name alive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ramoth, Anem—more Gershonite settlements, scattered across the northern kingdom to ensure no corner of Israel lacked access to the priestly ministry and music.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Asher came Mashal and Abdon—the western tribes too had their priestly cities, their sanctuaries of worship where the Lord was known and served.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hukok, Rehob—more Asherite cities, each one a seed of faith planted in the soil of Israel's inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kedesh in Galilee—famous as a city of refuge, its location in the North strategized for justice. Here Gershonites ensured the Lord's sanctuary extended even to the far reaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Merarites received Rimmon and Tabor in Zebulun—mountain and plains, each city a place where the third family of Levites could build their homes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beyond the Jordan—even the Trans-Jordan tribes, Reuben and Gad, received Merarite cities. Bezer was another city of refuge, where the Lord's mercy reached across the river.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kedemoth, Mephaath—Reubenite cities now devoted to priests and Levites, extending the reach of worship across the Jordan's eastern bank.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ramoth in Gilead—the great city east of Jordan, a fortress city of refuge, now also a beacon of priestly service in Gad's territory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Heshbon, Jazer—the final cities listed, completing a map of mercy and worship that spans all Israel from north to south, west to east. The priests lived where they were needed most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
